paras: The killing of Henry Seagraves was the shooting of a deputy United States marshal and revenue officer by a party of unidentified men in Macon County, Tennessee, on the night of April 8, 1881. The attackers robbed his body and escaped, and the collector of internal revenue at Nashville attributed the killing to Seagraves's part in breaking up illicit distilleries. The story ran as a wire item in daily papers from Washington to Savannah and as a one-line brief in rural weeklies.

Seagraves, whose family lived in Lafayette, had gone with a young man named Samuel Cox to collect money on executions, including at a new distillery, in or near Sumner County. On the way back they stopped for supper at the house of a Mr. Weatherford, between Eulia and Coatstown, about half a mile from the Sumner County line and twelve miles from Lafayette.

According to the particulars Collector W. M. Woodcock received, four men came to the cabin of a Black neighbor, asked whether the two officers had arrived, and fired two shots to draw them out. The official report to Commissioner Raum says that Seagraves, Cox and Weatherford walked toward the shots, and that when Seagraves asked who was there and gave his own name, the party fired and killed him instantly. The Nashville account gives the wounds as a shot through the heart and one through the right wrist, and says Cox fled while the host went back to the house.

The men then sent the neighbor to demand the officers' papers and money; in the Chicago Tribune's version he refused to bring Seagraves or drag the body to the cabin, while the revenue office account says they forced him to go. The attackers took Seagraves's watch, firearms, papers and money from the body, and the Tribune's correspondent reported that they "kept up a continuous yelling, and laughed and sang" as they did so. The neighbor did not know the men but thought they were from Sumner County and had followed the officers all day.

The body lay where it fell until the next day, when the coroner at Lafayette held an inquest, and it was then taken to Lafayette. Officials said every attempt was being made to find the killers, and an officer named Phillips thought that with enough men he could secure them. No report of an arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The first report was a Gallatin special to the Nashville American, printed in the Memphis Appeal on April 10 and in Washington, Savannah, Wheeling and Knoxville papers over the next two days. Headlines called it "A Revenue Officer Murdered" and "Cold-Blooded Murder," and the Chicago Tribune ran the fuller Nashville account as a "Cold-Blooded Assasination" by "assassins"; the same account reached the Louisiana Capitolian in Baton Rouge on April 14. Weekly papers, including the Richmond Democrat in Missouri, reduced the story to one sentence in a crime column, printed next to an item about vigilantes who had "summarily disposed of" three horse-thieves.

On April 20 Washington and Memphis papers carried the internal revenue office's report, which the National Republican printed under "Killing United States Officers" beside news of a captured North Carolina moonshiner. No paper gave Seagraves's race, and the only Black person in the accounts is the neighbor, identified as "a negro" or "a colored man."

The Gallatin dispatch said five men called Seagraves out of the farmhouse, took him to the woods and shot him twice through the head. The later accounts, built on reports gathered by revenue officials, describe four men or an unnumbered party who shot him near the neighbor's cabin without first moving him, and they disagree on the host's name, given as Weatherford or Rutherford.

bases: A party of four or five unidentified men shot and robbed a federal revenue officer at night, which officials attributed to his work against illicit distilleries; no paper reports a seizure under a claim of punishment, and no racial motive is reported (A6, A11, A12).

Seagraves was killed by four or five men acting without any authority (A5, A6, A12), but the papers describe an ambush and robbery of an officer, with the only motive offered being the collector's opinion that he was killed for breaking up illicit distilleries, not a claim of justice, race or tradition (A11).

The Gallatin dispatch (A1, A5) and the separate Nashville and internal revenue office accounts (A6, A10, A12) agree that Seagraves was shot dead at night in Macon County by a group of men, though they differ on details.
